ExtraaLearn: Lead Intelligence System¶

Practical Data Science | Elective Project¶

ExtraaLearn is an early-stage EdTech startup that sells technology programs to students and working professionals. As lead volume grows, so does the pressure to work the pipeline efficiently. The sales team can't chase everyone, so the question becomes: who is actually worth calling?

This project builds a Lead Intelligence System to answer that question:

  • Predict which leads are most likely to convert to paying customers
  • Identify what separates high-probability leads from low ones
  • Give the sales team a prioritized list of who to contact first

The full workflow runs from data understanding through EDA, preprocessing, modeling, explainability, lead scoring, and recommendations.

Appendix: Data Dictionary

Business Problem Overview¶

Industry Context¶

EdTech has grown fast, and competition for the same pool of learners has grown with it. Companies like ExtraaLearn can't rely on brand recognition or massive ad budgets to drive growth. Being efficient with how they allocate sales resources isn't optional -- it's the whole game.

The Problem¶

ExtraaLearn pulls in leads from multiple sources: the website, mobile app, social media, and referrals. The problem is there's no reliable signal for which leads are worth prioritizing. Treating every lead the same wastes the team's time on low-probability contacts while high-probability leads cool off waiting.

The central question: which leads are most likely to convert, and what do they look like?

Objective¶

  1. Predict which leads are most likely to become paying customers
  2. Identify the features that most influence conversion
  3. Profile what a high-conversion lead looks like
  4. Recommend how sales and marketing should adjust their approach

Solution Approach¶

Supervised binary classification on the ExtraaLearn lead dataset. Target variable is status (1 = converted, 0 = not converted).

Phase Focus
Data Understanding Structure, data types, quality checks, class split
EDA Conversion patterns by segment, engagement behavior, channel analysis
Preprocessing Encoding, scaling, outlier treatment, feature engineering
Modeling Logistic Regression through ensemble models with cross validation
Evaluation Precision, Recall, F1, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC
Explainability SHAP values, feature importance, business translation
Lead Scoring Probability-based tiers with action recommendations

Evaluation note: With a ~30% conversion rate, accuracy is a misleading metric. The final model is evaluated on ROC-AUC and PR-AUC, and output includes a scored lead list broken into priority tiers.

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

With the data confirmed clean, the focus shifts to understanding what is actually in it. EDA here is not just a formality, it is where the real business questions start to get answered.

The analysis is broken into two parts:

Univariate Analysis looks at each feature on its own. For numeric features this means understanding the shape of the distribution, the spread, and any obvious outliers. For categorical features it means understanding how the data is distributed across categories. This step builds the foundation for every decision made in preprocessing and modeling.

Multivariate Analysis looks at relationships between features and the target variable (status). The goal is to identify which features show the strongest signal for conversion, those findings directly inform feature selection and model interpretation later on.

The EDA is structured as follows:

  1. Target Distribution: class balance check for our target variable, status
  2. Univariate Analysis: Numeric Features
  3. Univariate Analysis: Categorical Features
  4. Correlation Analysis: Numeric Features
  5. Multivariate Analysis: Conversion Rates by Category
  6. Multivariate Analysis: Numeric Features vs. Conversion

Observations¶

The dataset is imbalanced with roughly 70% of leads not converting and 30% converting. This is expected for a lead funnel, most leads never become customers.

This split has direct implications for modeling:

  • Accuracy alone is not a useful metric here
  • Evaluation will focus on Precision, Recall, F1, and ROC-AUC
  • All classifiers will use class_weight='balanced' to avoid the model simply predicting the majority class

This imbalance is moderate enough that resampling techniques like SMOTE are not required, but it will be monitored throughout.

# Numeric Features: Distributions & Outliers
# Visualize the distribution of numeric features to understand their shape and identify outliers.
num_cols = data.select_dtypes(include=['float64', 'int64']).columns.drop('status')

# Boxplot stacked above histogram; mean (green dashed) and median (black solid) marked
def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(12, 7), kde=False, bins=None):
    fig, (ax_box, ax_hist) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,
        sharex=True,
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )
    sns.boxplot(data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box, showmeans=True, color="violet")

    hist_kwargs = {'data': data, 'x': feature, 'kde': kde, 'ax': ax_hist, 'color': 'steelblue'}
    if bins:
        hist_kwargs['bins'] = bins
    sns.histplot(**hist_kwargs)

    ax_hist.axvline(data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--")   # mean
    ax_hist.axvline(data[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-")  # median
    ax_box.set_title(
        f'{feature.replace("_", " ").title()} - Distribution & Outliers',
        fontsize=13, fontweight='bold'
    )
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def bar_plot(data, feature, figsize=(12, 7)):
    # stat='percent' normalizes the y-axis to show share of total
    plt.figure(figsize=figsize)
    ax = sns.countplot(data=data, x=feature, stat='percent')
    for p in ax.patches:
        ax.annotate(
            f'{p.get_height():.1f}%',
            (p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2., p.get_height()),
            ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold'
        )
    plt.title(f'{feature.replace("_", " ").title()} - Distribution', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
    plt.ylabel('Percentage')
    plt.xlabel(feature.replace('_', ' ').title())
    plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right')
    plt.show()

Observations¶

Current Occupation: The majority of leads (57%) identify as professionals. Unemployed leads make up the second largest group, followed by students. Together, unemployed and student leads account for less than half the total, meaning ExtraaLearn's audience skews heavily toward working adults.

First Interaction: Lead entry is fairly balanced between channels, with the website accounting for roughly 55% of first interactions and the mobile app making up the remaining 45%. Neither channel dominates significantly.

Profile Completion: The vast majority of leads have at least a partially completed profile. High and Medium completion are nearly equal at approximately 49% each, with Low completion representing only about 2% of leads. This suggests most leads are genuinely engaged enough to complete their profile.

Last Activity: Email activity accounts for nearly half (49%) of the most recent lead interactions, with phone and website activity at 27% and 24% respectively. Email is clearly the dominant touchpoint.

Media Exposure: Paid and earned media channels show very low reach across the board. Roughly 89% of leads were not exposed to newspaper ads, 95% not to magazine ads, 85% not to digital media, and 85% had no connection through educational channels. Referral was also minimal at approximately 98% No.

Key Takeaway: Most leads come in through owned channels -- the website and mobile app -- with paid and earned media touching a small fraction of the total. That puts more weight on behavioral signals like time on site, profile completion, and page views as potential predictors, since channel attribution alone won't tell the whole story. The multivariate analysis will test this.

Correlation Analysis¶

Numeric Features¶

In [55]:
# Correlation on original numeric features only -- engineered features evaluated separately
corr_matrix = data[num_cols.tolist() + ['status']].corr()

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))
sns.heatmap(corr_matrix,
            annot=True,
            fmt='.2f',
            cmap='coolwarm',
            vmin=-1,
            vmax=1,
            square=True
)
plt.title('Correlation Matrix: Numeric Features', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.show()

Observations¶

None of the numeric features have a strong linear relationship with status. time_spent_on_website comes in highest at +0.30, with age at +0.12. Meaningful signal, but neither clears the +/- 0.50 threshold typically associated with strong linear correlation.

Feature-to-feature correlations are all at 0.10 or below, which means these features aren't measuring the same thing and multicollinearity isn't a concern for Logistic Regression.

Low linear correlation doesn't mean low predictive value. The relationship between engagement and conversion is likely non-linear -- a lead spending 2,000 minutes on the site behaves very differently from one spending 50, but that gap won't show up cleanly in a Pearson correlation. That's exactly the kind of pattern tree-based models are built to find.

Note: This heatmap covers the original numeric features only. Engineered features and encoded categorical columns are evaluated separately.

# Create a function to look at categorical features against the target variable
def conversion_rate_plot(data, feature, figsize=(12,7)):
    plt.figure(figsize=figsize)
    
    # Calculate conversion rates
    conversion_rates = data.groupby(feature)['status'].mean().reset_index()
    
    # Bar plot of conversion rates
    ax = sns.barplot(data=conversion_rates, x=feature, y='status', palette='muted')

    for p in ax.patches:
        ax.annotate(
            f'{p.get_height() * 100:.1f}%',
            (p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2., p.get_height()),
            ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold'
        )
    
    plt.title(f'Conversion Rate by {feature.replace("_", " ").title()}', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
    plt.ylabel('Conversion Rate (%)')

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Observations¶

Current Occupation: Professionals have the highest conversion rate at 35.5%, followed by Unemployed at 26.6% and Students at 11.7%. Professionals convert at roughly 3x the rate of students, which likely reflects their financial position and motivation to invest in career development.

First Interaction: Leads whose first interaction was through the website convert at 45.6% compared to just 10.5% for the mobile app. This is one of the stronger signals in the dataset -- the channel of first contact appears to matter significantly.

Profile Completion: Conversion rates increase consistently with profile completion. High completion leads convert at 41.8%, Medium at 18.9%, and Low at 7.5%. Leads who invest more time completing their profile appear more committed to following through.

Last Activity: Website activity leads to the highest conversion rate at 38.5%, followed by email at 30.3% and phone at 21.3%. Active engagement with the website as the most recent touchpoint is a positive signal for conversion.

Media Exposure: Leads exposed to newspaper or magazine ads convert at roughly equal rates to each other. The same is true for digital media and educational channels. However, given that fewer than 15% of leads were reached through any of these channels, the impact on overall conversion volume is limited.

Referral: Referred leads convert at the highest rate of any category at 67.7%. While referrals make up only about 2% of all leads, the quality of those leads is clearly superior.

Key Takeaway: The strongest signals here are first_interaction, profile_completed, and referral. Professionals who came in through the website with a completed profile convert at dramatically higher rates. Referrals stand out at 67.7% -- small volume, but worth flagging as the highest-quality segment in the dataset.

With a base rate of ~30%, the numeric analysis and model will work out what behavioral patterns separate converters from everyone else.

Age¶

Website Visits¶

Time Spent On Website¶

Page Views Per Visit¶

Observations¶

Age: Leads that converted tend to fall in a tighter age range, with an IQR between 41 and 58 years old and a median around 54. Non-converted leads show a broader spread, with an IQR between 33 and 57. This suggests that more mature leads have a moderately higher tendency to convert, likely reflecting greater financial stability and career motivation. An interesting future opportunity would be identifying what it takes to get younger leads to convert earlier -- and potentially become repeat buyers -- though that is beyond the scope of this project.

Website Visits: Converted and non-converted leads show nearly identical medians and IQR for visit count, meaning visit frequency alone is not a strong signal. However, non-converted leads produced more high-end outliers, with some visiting up to 30 times compared to a max of 25 for converted leads. A lead visiting frequently without converting is an interesting behavioral pattern -- there is enough curiosity to keep returning, but something is preventing the decision to commit. Understanding what triggers that final conversion is a worthwhile question for the sales team.

Time Spent on Website: This is the strongest numeric signal in the dataset. Converted leads show a much higher time distribution, with an IQR between roughly 400 and 1800 minutes and a range up to 2,600 minutes. The majority of non-converted leads spent less time on the site than the median converted lead. Time on site reflects genuine engagement with the content, which appears to be a meaningful precursor to conversion.

Page Views per Visit: The pattern here closely mirrors website visits -- nearly identical distributions between converted and non-converted leads, with a similar outlier structure. This aligns with the low correlation we saw between these two features and the target in the correlation analysis. Neither metric alone is a strong differentiator, but both may contribute in combination with other features.

Key Takeaway: Time spent on the website is the clearest numeric predictor of conversion. Age shows a moderate signal favoring more mature leads. Visit count and page views are weaker on their own but may carry more weight as part of engineered composite features -- something we will explore in preprocessing. The pattern of high-frequency visitors who do not convert is worth flagging for the sales team as a potential re-engagement opportunity.

Note: The unit of measurement for time_spent_on_website is not explicitly defined in the data dictionary. For this analysis it is assumed to represent cumulative time in minutes across all visits per lead. The relative difference between converted and non-converted leads holds regardless of unit interpretation.

Preprocessing & Feature Engineering¶

EDA gave a clear picture of what needs attention before modeling. The steps here run in a logical order -- data quality first, then transformations, then the split.

  1. Missing Values: none found in the audit, documented here for the record
  2. Outlier Detection & Treatment: IQR method, cap extreme values rather than drop rows
  3. Skewness & Log Transformation: post-clipping skewness fell within acceptable bounds -- no log transform needed
  4. Feature Engineering: composite features to capture engagement patterns not visible in the raw columns
  5. Preprocessing Pipeline: ColumnTransformer (encoding + scaling)
  6. Train/Test Split: stratified 70/30 split

Missing Values¶

As noted earlier in the Data & Understanding Audit there were no missing values.

Outlier Detection & Treatment¶

In [60]:
# Loop through numeric columns: detect via IQR, clip in place if outliers exist
for num in num_cols:
    display(Markdown(f'#### {num.replace("_", " ").title()}'))
    Q1, Q3 = data[num].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    IQR = Q3 - Q1
    lower, upper = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR, Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
    outliers = ((data[num] < lower) | (data[num] > upper)).sum()
    pct = outliers / len(data) * 100
    print(f'Outliers detected: {outliers}')
    print(f'Lower bound: {lower:.2f} | Upper bound: {upper:.2f}')
    print(f'Outlier percentage: {pct:.2f}%')
    if outliers > 0:
        data[num] = data[num].clip(lower, upper)
        print(f'-> Clipped to IQR bounds')

age and time_spent_on_website came back clean. website_visits and page_views_per_visit both had outliers on the high end.

Treatment: Clipping (Winsorizing)

I clipped rather than dropped. Dropping rows means removing real leads -- a lead who visited 30 times isn't a data error, they're a highly engaged prospect and that record has real signal. Capping at the IQR upper bound keeps the record in the dataset while reducing the influence of extreme values on model training. Both features verified clean after treatment.

Skewness & Log Transformation¶

In [61]:
# Quantify the skewness of numeric features for potential log transformation
skewness = data[num_cols].skew().round(2)
for num in num_cols:
    print(f'{num}: Skewness = {skewness[num]}')

age: Skewness = -0.72
website_visits: Skewness = 0.89
time_spent_on_website: Skewness = 0.95
page_views_per_visit: Skewness = 0.2

Observations¶

Clipping the outliers in the previous step brought all four features within an acceptable skewness range -- capping the high-end values pulled the right tail in enough to resolve the issue without a log transform.

Skewness between -1 and 1 doesn't require log transformation. All four features land within that range after clipping, so no further treatment is needed here.

Note: Clipping changes real values -- a lead who visited 30 times and one who visited 9 times look the same after capping. For tree-based models this step is largely a non-issue since they handle extreme values naturally. The treatment matters more for Logistic Regression, which is sensitive to scale. Worth keeping in mind when comparing model results.

# Define categorical and numeric features for the preprocessor
cat_features = [
    'current_occupation', 'first_interaction',
    'profile_completed', 'last_activity'
]
num_features = [
    'age', 'website_visits', 'time_spent_on_website', 'page_views_per_visit',
    'marketing_touch_count', 'engagement_score', 'high_intent_flag',
    'print_media_type1', 'print_media_type2', 'digital_media',
    'educational_channels', 'referral'
]

# ColumnTransformer applies different transformations to different column groups
preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(transformers=[
    ('num', StandardScaler(), num_features),
    ('cat', OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore'), cat_features)
])

Observations¶

Three new features were engineered to capture patterns the raw columns don't express on their own:

Binary Encoding: The Yes/No media columns were mapped to 1/0 so they could be used in calculations. This was a prerequisite for the next step.

Marketing Touch Count: Sums exposure across newspaper, magazine, digital, and educational channels. A lead exposed to multiple channels is treated differently than one who saw nothing -- this single column captures that without adding four separate binary flags to the model.

Engagement Score: A composite of website visits, time on site, and page views, each normalized to a 0-1 scale before summing. Normalization was necessary because the three features operate on very different scales -- without it, time on site would dominate the score entirely.

High Intent Flag: Marks leads with both high profile completion and above-median time on site. 1,181 leads (25.6%) met both criteria. This captures a behavioral profile -- someone who invested time both setting up their profile and exploring the site -- that individual features alone wouldn't surface cleanly.

Train/Test Split¶

In [69]:
# Create train/test split
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42, stratify=y
)

# Verify the split
print(f'Training set: {X_train.shape} | Test set: {X_test.shape}')
print(f'Train conversion rate: {y_train.mean():.2%} | Test conversion rate: {y_test.mean():.2%}')

Training set: (3228, 16) | Test set: (1384, 16)
Train conversion rate: 29.86% | Test conversion rate: 29.84%
In [70]:
# Compute sample weights for class imbalance
# Used by Gradient Boosting, which does not support class_weight='balanced' directly
sample_weights = compute_sample_weight(
    class_weight='balanced',
    y=y_train
)

Observations¶

The data was split into a 70/30 train/test ratio with stratification applied on the target variable. Both sets maintained the original class distribution -- a 29.86% conversion rate in training and 29.84% in test -- confirming that the class imbalance is proportionally represented in each set. This is important for ensuring the model trains and evaluates on representative data.

Modeling¶

With preprocessing complete, the data is ready for modeling. The goal is to build a binary classifier that predicts whether a lead will convert, then identify the best performer through systematic comparison.

Four models are trained in order of complexity:

  1. Logistic Regression: baseline model, linear and interpretable
  2. Decision Tree: captures non-linear patterns, easy to visualize
  3. Random Forest: ensemble of trees, reduces overfitting through averaging
  4. Gradient Boosting: sequential ensemble, typically the strongest performer on tabular data

Each model is built inside a scikit-learn Pipeline that applies the preprocessing steps (encoding and scaling) automatically before training. This prevents data leakage and keeps the workflow clean and reproducible.

All classifiers use class_weight='balanced' to account for the 70/30 class imbalance in the target variable. Without this, a model that predicts "not converted" every time would appear to perform well on accuracy alone.

Model performance is evaluated using metrics suited for imbalanced classification: Precision, Recall, F1-Score, and ROC-AUC. Accuracy is tracked but not used as the primary decision metric.

The best-performing models are tuned further using cross-validated hyperparameter search before final evaluation.

In [71]:
# Helper: render a labelled confusion matrix for any fitted model
def show_confusion(y_true, y_pred, title):
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)
    disp = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(cm, display_labels=('Not Converted', 'Converted'))
    disp.plot(cmap='Blues')
    plt.title(title)
    disp.ax_.set_xlabel('Predicted')
    disp.ax_.set_ylabel('True')
    plt.show()

Logistic Regression¶

In [72]:
# Logistic Regression baseline (linear, interpretable)
lr_pipe = Pipeline(steps=[
    ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
    ('classifier', LogisticRegression(class_weight='balanced', random_state=42))
])

lr_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = lr_pipe.predict(X_test)

print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred))
print(f'ROC-AUC: {roc_auc_score(y_test, lr_pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]):.4f}')

show_confusion(y_test, y_pred, 'Confusion Matrix - Logistic Regression')

              precision    recall  f1-score   support

           0       0.91      0.79      0.85       971
           1       0.63      0.82      0.71       413

    accuracy                           0.80      1384
   macro avg       0.77      0.81      0.78      1384
weighted avg       0.83      0.80      0.81      1384

ROC-AUC: 0.8779

Observations¶

Baseline model. Recall (0.82) is the strongest part of the result -- the model catches most actual converters. Precision (0.63) is the tradeoff: about a third of the leads it flags as converters won't actually convert. F1 lands at 0.71 and ROC-AUC at 0.88, both reasonable for a first pass.

For this problem, leaning on recall is the right call. The cost of a false positive is a sales rep making an extra call that doesn't close. The cost of a false negative is missing a real customer entirely.

Note on class weight: I used class_weight='balanced' because the dataset is ~70/30 against the positive class. Without it, the model would happily predict "not converted" for everything and look fine on accuracy alone.

Decision Tree¶

In [73]:
# Decision Tree (captures non-linear splits, easy to inspect)
dt_pipe = Pipeline(steps=[
    ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
    ('classifier', DecisionTreeClassifier(class_weight='balanced', random_state=42))
])

dt_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = dt_pipe.predict(X_test)

print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred))
print(f'ROC-AUC: {roc_auc_score(y_test, dt_pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]):.4f}')

show_confusion(y_test, y_pred, 'Confusion Matrix - Decision Tree')

              precision    recall  f1-score   support

           0       0.87      0.85      0.86       971
           1       0.67      0.69      0.68       413

    accuracy                           0.81      1384
   macro avg       0.77      0.77      0.77      1384
weighted avg       0.81      0.81      0.81      1384

ROC-AUC: 0.7735

Observations¶

Decision Tree comes in weaker than Logistic Regression on the metrics that matter here. Recall dropped from 0.82 to 0.69, which means more real converters slip through. Precision ticked up slightly (0.67 vs 0.63), but that's a poor trade in this business context. ROC-AUC also fell to 0.77 -- a single tree just doesn't rank leads as well as a calibrated linear model on this data.

Moving on to ensembles to see if averaging across many trees fixes the recall problem without giving up the precision gains.

Random Forest¶

In [74]:
# Random Forest (bagged ensemble of trees)
rf_pipe = Pipeline(steps=[
    ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
    ('classifier', RandomForestClassifier(
        n_estimators=100,
        class_weight='balanced',
        random_state=42
    ))
])

rf_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = rf_pipe.predict(X_test)

print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred))
print(f'ROC-AUC: {roc_auc_score(y_test, rf_pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]):.4f}')

show_confusion(y_test, y_pred, 'Confusion Matrix - Random Forest')

              precision    recall  f1-score   support

           0       0.88      0.92      0.90       971
           1       0.79      0.70      0.74       413

    accuracy                           0.85      1384
   macro avg       0.83      0.81      0.82      1384
weighted avg       0.85      0.85      0.85      1384

ROC-AUC: 0.9142

Observations¶

Big jump in precision: 0.79, the best so far. Recall sits at 0.70 -- better than the single Decision Tree, still below Logistic Regression's 0.82. ROC-AUC of 0.91 is a clear step up and confirms the ensemble is ranking leads much better than either of the previous models.

The tradeoff is now between Logistic Regression (catch more converters, accept more false positives) and Random Forest (cleaner list, miss a few more). Worth seeing if boosting can deliver both.

Gradient Boosting (Tuned)¶

Tuning Gradient Boosting with GridSearchCV over learning rate, tree depth, number of estimators, subsample fraction, and min split/leaf size. Five-fold stratified CV keeps the class balance consistent across folds. Goal is to push ROC-AUC higher than the Random Forest baseline without trashing precision.

In [75]:
# Tuned Gradient Boosting via GridSearchCV
gb_pipe = Pipeline(steps=[
    ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
    ('classifier', GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=42))
])

param_grid = {
    'classifier__n_estimators': [100, 200, 300, 500],
    'classifier__learning_rate': [0.01, 0.05, 0.1],
    'classifier__subsample': [0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0],
    'classifier__max_depth': [2, 3, 4],
    'classifier__min_samples_split': [2, 5, 10],
    'classifier__min_samples_leaf': [1, 2, 4]
}

# Stratified CV preserves class balance in each fold
stratified_cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

gb_grid = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=gb_pipe,
    param_grid=param_grid,
    scoring='roc_auc',
    cv=stratified_cv,
    n_jobs=-1
)

gb_grid.fit(X_train, y_train, classifier__sample_weight=sample_weights)

print('Best Parameters:')
print(gb_grid.best_params_)
print(f'\nBest CV ROC-AUC: {gb_grid.best_score_:.4f}')

best_gb_model = gb_grid.best_estimator_
y_pred_gb = best_gb_model.predict(X_test)

print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred_gb))
roc_auc_gb = roc_auc_score(y_test, best_gb_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])
print(f'ROC-AUC: {roc_auc_gb:.4f}')

show_confusion(y_test, y_pred_gb, 'Confusion Matrix - Tuned Gradient Boosting')

Best Parameters:
{'classifier__learning_rate': 0.01, 'classifier__max_depth': 4, 'classifier__min_samples_leaf': 1, 'classifier__min_samples_split': 10, 'classifier__n_estimators': 500, 'classifier__subsample': 0.9}

Best CV ROC-AUC: 0.9273
              precision    recall  f1-score   support

           0       0.93      0.85      0.89       971
           1       0.71      0.85      0.77       413

weighted avg       0.86      0.85      0.85      1384

Observations¶

Tuned Gradient Boosting hits the sweet spot the earlier models couldn't. Recall climbs back to 0.85 (close to Logistic Regression's 0.82) and precision lands at 0.71 -- not as clean as Random Forest's 0.79, but the recall gain more than makes up for it. F1 of 0.77 and ROC-AUC of 0.93 are both the best results so far.

The selected hyperparameters tell a clear story: low learning rate (0.01) + 500 trees + depth 4 + 0.9 subsample. The model wants to learn slowly across many small trees rather than fast across a few deep ones, and pulling in 90% of rows per tree adds enough variance to keep it from memorizing the training set.

XGBoost (Tuned)¶

XGBoost is the next step up -- faster, more tuning knobs, and the go-to gradient boosting library in practice. It doesn't accept class_weight, so class imbalance is handled with scale_pos_weight instead.

Using RandomizedSearchCV here because the search space is large enough that an exhaustive grid would be wasteful. Fifty random combinations give good coverage at a fraction of the cost.

Tuning n_estimators, learning rate, depth, subsample, colsample_bytree, and scale_pos_weight. colsample_bytree is new -- it controls how many features each tree can see, which helps reduce overfitting.

In [76]:
# Imbalance ratio gives more weight to the converted leads during training
negative_count = (y_train == 0).sum()
positive_count = (y_train == 1).sum()
scale_pos_weight = negative_count / positive_count
print(f'Scale Pos Weight: {scale_pos_weight:.4f}')

xgb_pipe = Pipeline(steps=[
    ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
    ('classifier', XGBClassifier(
        objective='binary:logistic',
        eval_metric='logloss',
        random_state=42,
        n_jobs=-1
    ))
])

param_distributions = {
    'classifier__n_estimators': [100, 300, 500],
    'classifier__learning_rate': [0.01, 0.05, 0.1],
    'classifier__max_depth': [2, 3, 4],
    'classifier__subsample': [0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0],
    'classifier__colsample_bytree': [0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0],
    'classifier__scale_pos_weight': [
        1,
        scale_pos_weight * 0.75,
        scale_pos_weight,
        scale_pos_weight * 1.25
    ]
}

stratified_cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

xgb_random = RandomizedSearchCV(
    estimator=xgb_pipe,
    param_distributions=param_distributions,
    n_iter=50,
    scoring='roc_auc',
    cv=stratified_cv,
    n_jobs=-1,
    random_state=42,
    verbose=1
)

xgb_random.fit(X_train, y_train)

print('Best Parameters:')
print(xgb_random.best_params_)
print(f'\nBest CV ROC-AUC: {xgb_random.best_score_:.4f}')

best_xgb_model = xgb_random.best_estimator_
y_pred_xgb = best_xgb_model.predict(X_test)

print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred_xgb))
roc_auc_xgb = roc_auc_score(y_test, best_xgb_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])
print(f'ROC-AUC: {roc_auc_xgb:.4f}')

show_confusion(y_test, y_pred_xgb, 'Confusion Matrix - Tuned XGBoost')

{'classifier__subsample': 0.9, 'classifier__scale_pos_weight': np.float64(2.935684647302905), 'classifier__n_estimators': 100, 'classifier__max_depth': 4, 'classifier__learning_rate': 0.05, 'classifier__colsample_bytree': 0.7}

Observations¶

XGBoost ties tuned GB on F1 (0.77) but gets there with a different mix -- recall hits 0.88, the highest of any model, while precision drops to 0.69. ROC-AUC of 0.927 is essentially a tie with tuned GB (0.929).

The chosen params look reasonable: learning rate 0.05, depth 4, 100 trees, subsample 0.9, colsample_bytree 0.7. RandomizedSearchCV also picked a scale_pos_weight higher than the natural imbalance ratio (2.94 vs 2.35), which is what pushed recall up further.

Two more practical points worth flagging:

  1. XGBoost trained the full 50-iter randomized search much faster than the GB grid search ran. If retraining cadence matters, that's a real win.
  2. The recall/precision profile here favors the recall side harder than tuned GB. For lead scoring, that's likely the right shape.

Final Model Selection¶

Picking XGBoost as the final model.

Tuned GB edges it on ROC-AUC by 0.002, which isn't a meaningful gap. XGBoost wins on the metrics that matter for this problem:

  • Recall of 0.88 -- the strongest converter capture across all models
  • Much faster to train and retune, which matters if this gets put into any kind of refresh cadence

The extra false positives that come with higher recall are cheap here -- a sales rep makes an extra call that doesn't close. Missing a real converter is the expensive outcome, and XGBoost minimizes that better than anything else tested.

Model Evaluation¶

This section brings together the results from all models to confirm and visualize the decision to select XGBoost as the final model.

The evaluation includes:

  • Comparison table of key metrics
  • ROC curves: all models overlaid on a single chart
  • Precision-Recall curves: all models overlaid on a single chart

Results Comparison¶

In [77]:
# Build comparison table directly from the fitted models so it stays in sync
models = {
    'Logistic Regression': lr_pipe,
    'Decision Tree': dt_pipe,
    'Random Forest': rf_pipe,
    'Gradient Boosting (Tuned)': gb_grid.best_estimator_,
    'XGBoost (Tuned)': xgb_random.best_estimator_
}

rows = {}
for name, m in models.items():
    pred = m.predict(X_test)
    proba = m.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    rows[name] = {
        'Precision': precision_score(y_test, pred),
        'Recall': recall_score(y_test, pred),
        'F1': f1_score(y_test, pred),
        'Accuracy': (pred == y_test).mean(),
        'ROC-AUC': roc_auc_score(y_test, proba)
    }

model_comparison_df = pd.DataFrame(rows).T

# Highlight the best score per column
model_comparison_df.style.highlight_max(
    axis=0,
    props='background-color: #c6efce; color: #1a5c2e; font-weight: bold'
).format('{:.4f}')

Random Forest 0.7869 0.6973 0.7394 0.8533 0.9142

ROC Curves¶

In [78]:
# Reuse the same fitted models list across ROC and PR curves
eval_models = [
    ('Logistic Regression', lr_pipe),
    ('Decision Tree', dt_pipe),
    ('Random Forest', rf_pipe),
    ('Gradient Boosting (Tuned)', gb_grid.best_estimator_),
    ('XGBoost (Tuned)', xgb_random.best_estimator_)
]

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7))
for model_name, model in eval_models:
    y_pred_proba = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, y_pred_proba)
    auc_score = roc_auc_score(y_test, y_pred_proba)
    plt.plot(fpr, tpr, label=f'{model_name} AUC = {auc_score:.4f}')

plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle='--', color='grey', label='Random Classifier')
plt.title('ROC Curves by Model')
plt.xlabel('False Positive Rate')
plt.ylabel('True Positive Rate')
plt.legend(loc='lower right')
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

Observations¶

All four ensemble models cluster tightly between 0.91 and 0.93 ROC-AUC. Logistic Regression trails at 0.88 and Decision Tree lags well behind at 0.77.

The Decision Tree curve is visibly more angular than the others -- a single tree only has a handful of distinct probability values coming out of its leaf nodes, so the curve steps rather than smooths. The ensembles average predictions across many trees, which fills in the curve.

Precision-Recall Curves¶

In [79]:
# PR curves reuse the eval_models list defined above
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7))
for model_name, model in eval_models:
    y_pred_proba = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    precision, recall, _ = precision_recall_curve(y_test, y_pred_proba)
    pr_score = average_precision_score(y_test, y_pred_proba)
    plt.plot(recall, precision, label=f'{model_name} AP = {pr_score:.4f}')

# Baseline is the positive class rate (~0.30 here)
plt.axhline(y=0.30, linestyle='--', color='grey', label='Random Classifier Baseline')
plt.title('Precision-Recall Curves by Model')
plt.xlabel('Recall')
plt.ylabel('Precision')
plt.legend(loc='lower left')
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

Observations¶

Precision falls as recall rises across all models, which is expected -- as the threshold drops to capture more converters, more non-converters get pulled in too. The ensemble models hold their precision well into the high-recall zone, which is where this problem lives. Same angular pattern shows up in the Decision Tree curve for the same reason as the ROC plot.

Feature Importance & Explainability¶

SHAP is used to explain how each feature contributes to the model’s predictions. It shows which variables push a prediction higher or lower and how strongly they influence the outcome.

For this business problem, SHAP helps translate the XGBoost model from a prediction tool into something more actionable by showing what factors are most associated with lead conversion. This section reviews global feature importance across the model and then looks at individual predictions to understand what drives specific conversion outcomes.

In [80]:
# Extract the preprocessor and classifier from the final pipeline
preprocessor_step = best_xgb_model.named_steps["preprocessor"]

xgb_classifier = best_xgb_model.named_steps["classifier"]

# Transform X_test using the fitted preprocessor
X_test_transformed = preprocessor_step.transform(X_test)

# Get feature names after preprocessing / encoding
feature_names = preprocessor_step.get_feature_names_out()
In [81]:
# Convert transformed X_test into a DataFrame so SHAP keeps feature names
X_test_transformed_df = pd.DataFrame(
    X_test_transformed,
    columns=feature_names,
    index=X_test.index
)

# Build SHAP explainer and calculate SHAP values
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(xgb_classifier)
shap_values = explainer(X_test_transformed_df)
In [82]:
# Create SHAP plots
shap.plots.bar(shap_values)
shap.plots.beeswarm(shap_values)

SHAP Observations¶

The bar plot ranks features by mean absolute SHAP value -- a clean view of which features move the model's predictions the most, regardless of direction. The beeswarm plot adds the direction back in by showing how each feature's actual values translate into push toward or away from conversion.

Top drivers of conversion:

  • time_spent_on_website -- most influential overall, with longer sessions pushing predictions toward conversion
  • first_interaction = Website -- web-first leads convert at higher rates than mobile-first ones
  • profile_completed = High -- complete profiles are a strong positive signal
  • current_occupation = Professional -- professionals convert more than students or unemployed leads
  • high_intent_flag -- the engineered feature paid off, it's near the top

Pushing the other direction:

  • first_interaction = Mobile App and last_activity = Phone Activity both consistently lower the conversion probability
  • profile_completed = Medium doesn't help either -- partial signals look more like noise than commitment

The story is straightforward: leads who showed up via the website, filled out their profile, and spent real time on the site are the ones worth calling first. Mobile and phone-only patterns need more nurturing before they're ready.

Lead Scoring & Priority Tiers¶

The XGBoost model outputs a probability for every lead. A binary predict/don't-predict answer throws most of that signal away -- a lead at 0.91 and a lead at 0.51 both come back as "yes" and the sales team can't tell them apart. Bucketing the predicted probabilities into Hot, Warm, Nurture, and Low tiers preserves the ranking, gives reps a prioritized list, and makes the threshold choices explicit instead of hidden inside the model.

In [83]:
# Score the test set with the final XGBoost model
test_probs = best_xgb_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

# Bin probabilities into priority tiers
# right=False so 0.75 lands in Hot, 0.50 in Warm, 0.25 in Nurture
tier_bins = [0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.01]
tier_labels = ['Low', 'Nurture', 'Warm', 'Hot']

lead_scores = pd.DataFrame({
    'actual': y_test.values,
    'probability': test_probs,
    'tier': pd.cut(test_probs, bins=tier_bins, labels=tier_labels, right=False, include_lowest=True)
}, index=X_test.index)

Observations¶

The tier conversion rates land exactly where they should: Hot at 79.9%, Warm at 40.7%, Nurture at 14.9%, Low at 1.4%. EEach tier clears the next one by a clean margin, and only Hot and Warm sit above the 29.8% base rate. That's real separation -- the model isn't just predicting, it's ranking.

For the sales team: Hot is 27% of the pipeline and captures 73% of the actual converters. Working that bucket first means roughly three out of four real customers come from less than a third of the lead volume. Warm is the second pass -- still well above base rate at 41%, worth working but with lower expected yield per call.

For Nurture: 15% conversion is below base rate but it's not noise. These leads have real but incomplete signal -- partial profile, lower engagement, or both. The right move is automation: drip email, retargeting, or a delayed second touch. Cheap to keep warm, not cheap enough to call cold.

Low at 1.4% is essentially dead. Don't spend sales time here. If marketing wants to keep them in a long-cycle nurture program that's fine, but they're not a sales priority.

Recommendations¶

The model and SHAP analysis surface specific patterns about what separates converting leads from the rest. This section translates those findings into actions for the three teams closest to the result: sales (how to work the pipeline), marketing (where to put acquisition spend), and product (what the behavior tells us about the onboarding experience).

In [87]:
# Validate high_intent_flag conversion lift on the test set
# (cell 83 ran this on the full dataset -- this confirms the signal holds on test)
test_lift = pd.DataFrame({
    'high_intent_flag': X_test['high_intent_flag'].values,
    'converted': y_test.values
})

flag_summary = test_lift.groupby('high_intent_flag')['converted'].agg(
    lead_count='size',
    conversion_rate='mean'
)
flag_summary['conversion_rate'] = (flag_summary['conversion_rate'] * 100).round(1)
flag_summary.index = ['Low Intent', 'High Intent']

flag_summary
Out[87]:
lead_count conversion_rate
Low Intent 1026 21.30
High Intent 358 54.20

Sales¶

  • Work the Hot tier first, every day. It's 27% of the pipeline and captures 73% of real converters. SLA the response time -- ideally first contact within 24 hours of the lead crossing 0.75.
  • Warm tier (40.7% conversion) is the second pass. Real opportunity, lower yield per call. Slot into the calendar after Hot is cleared.
  • Don't manually work Nurture or Low. Hand them to marketing automation. The probability score is already a routing decision -- use it.
  • Use the raw probability for tie-breaks within Hot. A lead at 0.94 and one at 0.76 are both Hot, but they're not the same. Call the higher one first.

Marketing¶

  • Website-first acquisition outperforms Mobile App-first acquisition. Conversion likelihood drops noticeably when the first touch is the mobile app. Shift acquisition spend toward channels that drive web traffic (search, referral programs, educational content) and reassess what's driving mobile-app installs that don't convert.
  • Profile completion is the single highest-leverage signal after engagement. Build the acquisition funnel to push profile completion early -- the leads that finish their profile are the ones the model picks up. Half-completed profiles read as noise to the model and don't help sales either.
  • Nurture tier needs an automated drip. 15% conversion is below base rate but well above zero. Cheap to keep warm with email and retargeting, expensive to ignore entirely.

Product¶

  • Time on site is the top SHAP feature. Look at what content keeps high-intent leads on the site longer and surface it earlier in the journey. If onboarding pages are bouncing fast, time-on-site is measuring noise instead of intent.
  • Investigate the mobile app onboarding flow. Mobile-first leads convert worse than web-first leads. This could be UX friction, feature parity, or a different audience -- worth a separate funnel analysis. Right now it looks like the mobile app is a leak.
  • Surface the high-intent signal in-product. The engineered high_intent_flag (high profile completion + above-median time on site) captures something real -- 54% conversion vs 22% for the rest. Use it to trigger in-app prompts: assigning a rep, surfacing pricing, offering a demo at the moment the signal fires.

Conclusions & Executive Summary¶

ExtraaLearn's sales team is working a growing pool of leads with no reliable way to tell which ones are worth calling first. Treating every lead the same wastes time on prospects who won't convert and lets real customers cool off in the queue. This project built a Lead Intelligence System that takes the raw lead data ExtraaLearn already collects -- demographics, site behavior, channel exposure, profile completion -- and turns it into a prioritized list with a probability score for every lead. The result is a sales workflow built around the leads most likely to convert, not the leads that happen to land in the queue first.

Key Findings¶

Engagement is the strongest signal in the data. Time spent on the website is the most influential feature across every model, and it shows up as the top SHAP driver in the final XGBoost model. Leads who spend real time on the site convert at a meaningfully higher rate than those who don't, regardless of how they were acquired.

Profile completion separates serious leads from casual ones. Leads who fully completed their profile converted at much higher rates than those who only partially filled it out. The engineered high_intent_flag -- a combination of high profile completion and above-median time on site -- captured this pattern in a single feature and converted at roughly 2.5x the rate of leads without the flag.

How a lead first interacts with ExtraaLearn matters more than how much marketing they see. First interaction through the website is consistently associated with higher conversion than first interaction through the mobile app, while paid channels (print, digital, educational) show only weak signal on conversion. The acquisition channel that gets a lead to the website -- and into a real session -- is more valuable than the channel that simply gets a lead's attention.

Final Model¶

XGBoost was selected as the final model. On the held-out test set it achieved:

  • Recall of 0.88 -- of all the leads that actually converted, the model correctly identified 88% of them
  • Precision of 0.69 -- of the leads the model flagged as converters, 69% actually did
  • ROC-AUC of 0.927 -- strong ranking ability, the model reliably scores real converters higher than non-converters

The metric that matters most here is recall. A false positive -- a lead that gets called and doesn't close -- costs the sales team a few minutes. A false negative -- a real customer who never gets prioritized -- costs ExtraaLearn the entire deal. The model is tuned to lean toward catching converters, accepting some extra outreach in exchange for missing fewer real opportunities.

XGBoost edged out tuned Gradient Boosting by a fraction on ROC-AUC, but the bigger wins were stronger recall (0.88 vs 0.85) and significantly faster training time, which matters if the model gets retrained on a regular cadence as new lead data comes in.

Lead Scoring Output¶

The final deliverable is a tiering system that turns every model probability into a sales action. Leads are scored on a 0-1 probability and bucketed into Hot (≥ 0.75), Warm (0.50-0.74), Nurture (0.25-0.49), and Low (< 0.25). On the test set, conversion rates landed at 80%, 41%, 15%, and 1% respectively -- each tier well-separated from the next. The Hot tier alone accounted for 27% of the pipeline and captured 73% of all actual converters, meaning the sales team can focus on just over a quarter of incoming leads and still capture three out of four real customers.

Limitations & Caveats¶

A few things worth flagging before this gets put into production:

  • Single-slice evaluation. The model was trained and tested on one snapshot of the data. Lead behavior, channel mix, and the base conversion rate can all shift over time. The model should be retrained on a regular cadence and performance monitored once it's live -- a drift in any of these will degrade the tier accuracy.
  • SHAP explains the model, not the business. SHAP shows which features the model leans on, not which features cause conversion. "Mobile app first interaction" being a negative signal in the model doesn't prove the mobile app causes leads to drop off -- it could be that the audience landing on the app is different from the audience landing on the web. The Product team recommendation to investigate the mobile flow stands, but the finding is a starting point, not a verdict.
  • Marketing channel signal is weak. The model didn't find much predictive value in the print, digital, or educational channel flags. That could mean those channels genuinely don't drive conversion, or it could mean the way exposure is being tagged isn't capturing what actually matters. Worth a data-quality pass on how marketing exposure is being recorded before drawing conclusions about channel ROI.

Appendix: Data Dictionary¶

Original Features¶

Column Type Description
ID string Unique lead identifier. Dropped before modeling — no predictive value.
age int Lead age in years. Range: 18–63.
current_occupation categorical Employment status: Professional, Student, Unemployed.
first_interaction categorical Channel of first contact: Website, Mobile App.
profile_completed categorical Profile completion level: High, Medium, Low.
website_visits int Number of visits to the ExtraaLearn website. Outliers clipped at IQR upper bound (9.5).
time_spent_on_website int Total time spent on the website across all visits. Unit assumed to be minutes — not explicitly defined in the source data. Outliers: none detected.
page_views_per_visit float Average pages viewed per website visit. Outliers clipped at IQR upper bound (6.27).
last_activity categorical Most recent interaction type: Website Activity, Email Activity, Phone Activity.
print_media_type1 binary Exposed to Type 1 print advertising (newspaper). Original: Yes/No. Encoded: 1/0.
print_media_type2 binary Exposed to Type 2 print advertising (magazine). Original: Yes/No. Encoded: 1/0.
digital_media binary Exposed to digital media advertising. Original: Yes/No. Encoded: 1/0.
educational_channels binary Reached through educational channel advertising. Original: Yes/No. Encoded: 1/0.
referral binary Lead came through a referral. Original: Yes/No. Encoded: 1/0.
status binary Target variable. 1 = converted to paying customer, 0 = not converted. Class split: 70.1% not converted, 29.9% converted.

Engineered Features¶

Column Type Description
marketing_touch_count int Sum of the four binary media exposure columns (print_media_type1, print_media_type2, digital_media, educational_channels). Captures breadth of marketing channel exposure. Range: 0–4.
engagement_score float MinMax-scaled composite of website_visits, time_spent_on_website, and page_views_per_visit, summed into a single value. Captures overall behavioral engagement. Range: 0–3.
high_intent_flag binary 1 if profile_completed = High AND time_spent_on_website > dataset median, else 0. Identifies leads showing both commitment (profile) and engagement (time on site). Test set conversion rate: 54.2% (flag = 1) vs 21.3% (flag = 0).
